## Claude Code vs. Codex: Loops, Graphs, and Harnesses

This is a casual pair-programming meetup for developers experimenting with Claude Code, Codex, and agentic coding workflows.
There is no formal presentation and no fixed curriculum. Bring a laptop, a repository, a side project, or a workflow you want to test. We will work in small groups, compare approaches, debug problems, and share what is working.

Possible areas to explore include:

* Building iterative coding-agent loops
* Comparing Claude Code and Codex on the same task
* Designing graph-based agent workflows
* Creating reusable coding harnesses
* Managing context across large repositories
* Running tests and validating agent-generated changes
* Using sandboxes, permissions, and approval steps
* Coordinating subagents or parallel tasks
* Measuring latency, token usage, cost, and completion quality
* Debugging failed or incomplete agent runs

You do not need to be an expert in either tool. This meetup is for people who want hands-on time to experiment, pair with other developers, and learn through building.
Bring something you are working on, or join someone else’s project.

name: AI Governance Overview: What’s Happening in International AI Competition?
description:
**A free, 90-minute online workshop—no technical background needed**
AI is moving fast. The companies building it are moving fast. And the countries racing to lead in AI, especially the US and China, are moving fast too. Governments are trying to respond, but most people still don't have a clear picture of what is actually happening, or what good policy would even look like. This workshop gives you that bigger picture.
We'll start with a quick, plain-English overview of what AI is, how today's systems work at a high level, and why the last few years have felt so different from earlier AI progress. From there, we'll look at the industry forming around the most advanced AI: the major labs, the incentives they face, the race to build more capable models, and why that race, now as much between countries as between companies, has raised serious questions about safety and governance.
Then we'll turn to AI safety: what people mean by it, why it matters, and why it isn't just a technical issue for researchers in labs. AI already causes real problems today, from scams and misinformation to bias, privacy concerns, cyber risks, and job disruption. More advanced models could raise the stakes further, especially if they get better at persuasion, hacking, autonomous planning, scientific research, or acting on people's behalf in the real world.
Together, we'll explore questions like:

* **What is AI, really?** What makes today's systems different from older software, and why are people treating this moment as a major technological shift?
* **What is AI safety?** What are researchers, policymakers, and companies worried about, and which concerns are immediate versus longer-term?
* **Current risks:** How is AI already affecting scams, misinformation, privacy, jobs, education, and trust?
* **Near-future risks:** What could change if AI becomes significantly more capable over the next year or two?
* **International competition:** How are the US, China, and other countries competing for the lead in AI, through chips, export controls, and massive investment, and what does that race mean for safety?
* **AI legislation:** What laws and regulations have been passed so far, what are they trying to do, and how has the debate around them played out?
* **Governance options:** What policy tools are being discussed to handle more serious risks from advanced AI, and could rival countries ever agree on shared rules?

**What you'll get:**

* A beginner-friendly overview of AI as a technology and an industry
* A clear explanation of what AI safety means and why people disagree about it
* A grounded look at the risks AI poses today and the risks more advanced systems may pose soon
* A concrete overview of existing AI policy efforts and the debate around them
* A look at the global AI race: who the main players are, what's driving them, and why international cooperation is so hard
* A map of the main governance ideas being discussed, from transparency and safety testing to liability, licensing, compute governance, and international coordination

This workshop isn't about taking a simple "AI good" or "AI bad" position. The real world is messier than that.
AI could bring enormous benefits, and it could also create serious problems if we build and deploy it carelessly. The goal is to help you understand the policy conversation well enough to follow what's happening, evaluate proposals for yourself, and think clearly about what responsible governance might look like, at home and between nations, before the technology gets even more powerful.

name: What AI Can Do With Your Data: Privacy & Surveillance
description:
**A free, 90-minute online workshop—no technical background needed**
Most of us already know that companies, governments, and apps collect a lot of data about us. That part isn't new.
**What *is* new is what AI makes possible with that data.**
For years, the privacy conversation has mostly been about tracking, ads, data brokers, social media, and surveillance. Those concerns still matter. But AI changes the picture: once powerful models can analyze huge amounts of text, images, location data, purchases, messages, and online behavior at scale, personal data becomes far more valuable, and far riskier.
This workshop looks at how data and privacy worked before AI, and what changes now that AI systems can search, summarize, infer, predict, and act on massive amounts of personal information.
Together, we'll explore questions like:

* **Surveillance:** How could AI make it easier to monitor people, spot patterns, and draw conclusions from huge amounts of data?
* **Incentives:** Why might companies and governments have stronger reasons than ever to collect, store, and analyze personal information?
* **Advertising and persuasion:** How could AI make targeted ads, political messaging, and behavioral manipulation more personalized and more effective?

**What you'll get:**

* A clear, beginner-friendly overview of how data privacy worked before modern AI
* A practical explanation of why AI changes the value and the danger of personal data
* Real examples of how AI is already being used in surveillance, advertising, and persuasion
* A framework for thinking clearly about privacy, power, and trust in a world where data is easier than ever to analyze

This isn't a workshop about deleting every app or becoming paranoid about technology. It's about understanding the new reality we're entering.
AI doesn't just make data more useful. It makes data more actionable. That means the privacy choices we make, as individuals, companies, and societies, are going to matter a lot more than they used to.

name: (CS)²AI Online: Cyber-Informed Engineering (CIE):  Bridging the OT Divide
description:
**Control systems are under constant threat, and patching and monitoring alone can’t stop an attacker who is determined and well resourced. Cyber-Informed Engineering (CIE) takes a different approach. It builds security into how systems are designed and operated, so the worst consequences can be engineered out.**

**Join Virginia “Ginger” Wright, CIE Program Manager at Idaho National Laboratory, for a session on what CIE looks like in practice. Ginger leads INL’s work on the DOE National Strategy for CIE and wrote the CIE Implementation Guide. She has also testified before the U.S. Senate on the subject.**
**You’ll leave with:**

* **A clear grounding in CIE. The session starts with a quick primer, so no background is needed.**
* **A current view of the threats to control systems. You’ll see what adversaries are doing now and why traditional defenses fall short.**
* **A real-world case study. It shows how CIE thinking changes outcomes.**
* **Hands-on knowledge of the tools for applying CIE. The main focus is how to use them, including the Engineering Controls Database.**

**Who should attend: ICS/OT security practitioners, control systems and process engineers, IT/OT convergence teams, asset owners and operators, security leaders, and anyone building a career in critical infrastructure protection.**

***Whether you’re an engineer learning security or a security professional learning engineering, this session gives you methods you can use right away.***

Jitsi Meet agenda:

Q&A with emcee CJ Fearnley from 7-7:30PM. Bring your Linux (and related) questions for a group exploration.

The main presentation from 7:30-8:30PM: TBD.

University of the Sciences in Philadelphia (USP)
Griffith Hall (Room "A" or "C", look for the signs)
600 South 43rd Street

Often, the door to Griffith Hall is locked at 7PM. If you find the door locked, please contact the security guard (usually in the booth in the parking lot) and tell them that the monthly PLUG (Philadelphia Linux User Group) meeting in Griffith Hall is tonight. If there is no one in the booth you can call UCS's public safety number at 215.895.1117 and they will radio personnel to unlock the door. Our sponsor is Zhiwei Liu in the Chemistry department. Security knows this and will almost always open the door for you and have it unlocked so other participants can enter without issue.

name: Who Gets a Say in AI? Mapping the Power and Your Place in It
description:
**A free, 90-minute online workshop—no technical background needed**
AI is rapidly reshaping society, but a small number of companies, researchers, and political actors currently have outsized influence over where this technology goes next. The question is: who gets a say in the future of AI, and how can ordinary people meaningfully influence it?
This workshop explores the competing visions currently shaping AI development, from Silicon Valley accelerationism to AI safety advocates, governments, artists, workers, and the broader public.
Together, we'll discuss questions like:

* Who is currently guiding the direction of AI technology, and what do they want?
* What kinds of futures are being prioritized, and which voices are missing from the conversation?
* How should AI be developed, deployed, and integrated into society?
* How can individuals and communities actually influence the trajectory of AI?

**What you'll get:**

* A beginner-friendly overview of the major groups shaping AI today
* Interactive discussions about what kind of AI future you want to see
* Practical pathways for getting involved, from public advocacy to local organizing and community building

Come ready to think critically about one of the most important technologies of our time, and where your voice fits into the conversation about humanity's future with AI.

name: Cheers & Ideas: ProductTank Philly Holiday Party & White Elephant Exchange 🎁🍻
description:
Let’s wrap up 2026 with good vibes, great people, and a drink (or two)!
Join **ProductTank Philadelphia** for our annual **Cheers & Ideas Holiday Party**—a casual evening to celebrate another year in product, connect with fellow product thinkers, and help shape what’s next for our community in 2027.

And this year, we’re adding a little something special: a **Product White Elephant Exchange! 🎁**

**📅 Wednesday, December 9, 2026**
**🕡 6:30–8:30 PM**
**📍 City Winery Philadelphia**

### **🎁 Introducing the Product White Elephant Exchange!**

Think traditional White Elephant gift exchange meets product management and marketing.

The challenge: Bring a wrapped gift ($5-10 max), but instead of guessing what’s inside, prepare to give a short product description or marketing pitch that describes and sells other participants but doesn’t name what is inside..
Your mission? Make your gift sound like the next must-have product.
Think exaggerated value propositions, creative positioning, clever marketing language, or even intentionally misleading (but technically accurate) product descriptions.

Minute-of, AI generated product pitches (without giving the product name away) also welcomed for added fun and potential humor.

**For example:**
A simple coffee mug becomes: “*A portable, reusable liquid containment platform designed to optimize daily productivity and enhance the user experience through seamless integration with your preferred stimulant delivery system.*”

We’ll exchange gifts White Elephant-style, with participants choosing and stealing gifts based on the pitches before opening. Participation is completely optional, but if you want to join the exchange, bring one wrapped gift with your product messaging ready. Keep the actual gift a surprise!

We're also planning an additional raffle for a Product Management item that will help in your year to come!

### **🍻 Come if you:**

→ Survived 2026 and have stories to prove it
→ Want to meet Philly product people
→ Have strong opinions about roadmaps, frameworks, AI, or literally anything
→ Think you could market a $10 gift like a billion-dollar startup
→ Need a break from your backlog
→ Want to help shape what ProductTank Philly does in 2027

### **✨ What to expect:**

**🍻 Drinks & good company** — Because some of the best product conversations happen outside the office.
**🎁 Product White Elephant Exchange** — A little creative positioning, questionable value propositions, and friendly competition.
**💡 Ideas for 2027** — Help us dream up next year’s ProductTank events. No formal planning session, just good conversations and ideas.
**🤝 Your people** — PMs, marketers, founders, designers, engineers, and the whole Philly product community.
**🎉 A few surprises** — We’ll have a raffle and some fun swag giveaways, too!

Bring your hot takes. Bring your war stories. Bring your ideas for 2027. And, if you’re feeling adventurous, **bring a wrapped product with a pitch that would make even your product marketing team proud.**

### **A Few Notes**

* **Each guest will cover their own food and drinks.**
* **The Product White Elephant Exchange is optional - no gift is needed if you’re just joining us to celebrate and socialize.**

**We hope to see you there!**

From understanding how AI is transforming in-demand roles to benchmarking compensation and exploring smarter workforce strategies, we'll break down what the latest data tells us —and what you can do with it.

**[🔗 We'll also break down key market and workforce insights from Motion's 2027 Tech Salary Guide](https://motionrecruitment.com/it-salary-tech-in-motion)**

**Key Takeaways**

* **The skills shaping 2027**: Which technical capabilities are gaining momentum as AI and emerging technologies reshape the workforce.
* **The roles evolving fastest:** How expectations are changing across software engineering, data, product, and other tech disciplines.
* **The compensation landscape**: Where salaries are moving, which skills are driving premiums, and how to benchmark your position in the market.
* **The opportunities ahead**: How to identify career growth opportunities, strengthen your competitive edge, and make more informed talent decisions.
* **A plan for what's next**: Practical ways to translate market data into career development, hiring, and workforce planning strategies.

name: PLUG Central - Jitsi Meet: 7-9PM; Speaker from 7:30-8:30PM
description:
Please join us for PLUG Central. During the pandemic we meet on-line at Jitsi Meet, beginning at 7pm. RSVPs are optional. Anyone interested in Linux and Free and Open Source software is welcome to attend. We welcome all levels of expertise, whether you're just curious, a hobbyist, or a professional.

Jitsi Meet agenda:

Q&A with emcee CJ Fearnley from 7-7:30PM. Bring your Linux (and related) questions for a group exploration.

The main presentation from 7:30-8:30PM: TBD.

Q&A continued from 8:30-9PM.

After the pandemic dissipates, we plan to again meet in Lecture Hall A in Griffith Hall at USP in Philadelphia. We plan to revert to the original speaker slot from 8-9PM with Q&A at the beginning to better support travel constraints.

After the presentation some of us adjourn to Clarkville (http://www.clarkvillephilly.com/) a nearby pizza and craft beer restaurant.

University of the Sciences in Philadelphia (USP)
Griffith Hall (Room "A" or "C", look for the signs)
600 South 43rd Street
Philadelphia, PA 19104-4495

USP is located in University City. Driving directions are available at http://www.phillylinux.org/locations/usp.html, or http://www.usip.edu/directions, both of which have an aerial view of the campus buildings. USP is also easily accessible by public transportation.

Often, the door to Griffith Hall is locked at 7PM. If you find the door locked, please contact the security guard (usually in the booth in the parking lot) and tell them that the monthly PLUG (Philadelphia Linux User Group) meeting in Griffith Hall is tonight. If there is no one in the booth you can call UCS's public safety number at 215.895.1117 and they will radio personnel to unlock the door. Our sponsor is Zhiwei Liu in the Chemistry department. Security knows this and will almost always open the door for you and have it unlocked so other participants can enter without issue.
